Sophie Mirabella I rise to speak on the so-called Australian Jobs Bill 2013. In doing so I wish to express my frustration with not only the content of the bill but the government's lack of accountability in explaining and justifying the reasons for its introduction and its apparent determination to yet again push through legislation that will increase regulatory and compliance costs for Australian businesses. Given that it has misled the Australian people hundreds and hundreds of times, it is difficult to take almost anything that this government says at face value. But it is even harder to find reason to support one of its bills when there is so little clarification around even the very basic details in the legislation—the precise reasons for the change and exactly how those changes will be financed. Prior to February this year, I cannot recall in my time as a shadow minister ever having been refused a briefing by the government. In February was when my office asked Minister Combet's office if I could receive a briefing from the government following the release of the so-called Industry Innovation Statement—otherwise described as a 'jobs plan', another Orwellian phrase—of which these changes form a part. That request was pointedly refused. One of a number of reasons why I sought that briefing was to try and obtain more detail about the changes to which this bill potentially would give effect. Such conduct points not only to a disturbing lack of accountability on the part of the minister but also to a complete arrogant disregard for accepted protocol, good governance and accountability—especially when a staff member in the minister's office tells a staff member in mine that the basic reason for the refusal is that I apparently had the temerity, the gall, the nerve, to make some public criticisms of a number of elements of the government's policies in this area. Richard Colbeck Prior to question time I was making some comments in relation to the Australian Jobs Bill 2013. In my comments I did not say that the opposition are opposing this piece of legislation, but I did put on the record some of the reasons why we might be doing that. One reason in particular is that this legislation imposes additional costs on industry and on business, which, as I said earlier, is a hallmark of this government. I talked about the fact that this government has imposed the carbon tax on Australian business. The government claims that it has only a small impact, but it does its calculations on an economy-wide basis—it ignores sectoral specifics of the cost of a carbon tax on industry. I know one business, for example, that has spent $17 million to mitigate the cost of the carbon tax on its business. It did receive some government assistance to put a co-generation plant in as a part of that project. That will reduce their energy costs, but not in a net sense. After they have spent that $17 million, after they have received $4 million in taxpayers' assistance to spend that money, they will still have a $7 million a year bill over and above what they had before the carbon tax came in. The government talks about its food and foundries program. Government members were in Wynyard in Tasmania with a company recently, talking about the fact that that company was going to save $140,000 a year on its energy bills, but they did not say what the net cost to the company of the energy bills was. That is what the opposition has been complaining about the whole time: the government talks about the saving but it does not talk about what the overall cost is going to be. As I said, one business spent $17 million to reduce its energy costs, which it has done, but in a net sense it is still $7 million a year worse off. Criticised the Australian Jobs Bill 2013, revealing her office was refused a ministerial briefing in February after publicly criticising the government's Industry Innovation Statement, disputed the government's claim of a $1 billion research and development funding cut as unverified, and cited more than 140,000 net manufacturing job losses under this government, one every 19 minutes, against 6,000 to 7,000 lost over 11½ years under the Howard government.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill 2013, requiring Australian Industry Participation Plans for projects worth $500 million or more, estimating it could generate up to $6.4 billion in economic activity, and detailed a $24.4 million investment to nearly double antidumping investigators and 10 new industry innovation precincts, while warning a coalition government would cut $500 million from the New Car Plan, with a further $1.5 billion cut planned, threatening 200,000 auto sector jobs.

Rejected the government's approach, saying the coalition would immediately repeal the carbon tax and dismissing the Australian Jobs Bill's title as another example of the government's Orwellian naming of legislation that will not actually create jobs.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill as part of a $1 billion package launched on 17 February, citing modelling showing it could generate $1.6 billion to $6.4 billion in additional work for Australian firms, and highlighted the Tonsley Park redevelopment in her Kingston electorate following Mitsubishi's 2008 closure, noting one in 10 of the nation's manufacturing workers live in her electorate.

Opposed the bill, citing ABS figures showing 682,900 Australians unemployed as of April 2013, an increase of 211,000 or 45 per cent since the government took office, against population growth of 1,858,000, and noted the Treasurer's promised 500,000 new jobs this financial year has delivered only 123,000, while warning the carbon tax will extend to trucking diesel from 1 July 2014, adding 7 cents a litre.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill, noting manufacturing makes up about 8.3 per cent of employment and 8.6 per cent of GDP yet contributes more than 25 per cent of business R&D investment, cited Australian Steel Institute estimates that local steel wins only 10 to 12 per cent of major resource project work, and credited the $300 million Steel Transformation Plan with keeping BlueScope open.

Opposed the Australian Jobs Bill, noting the existing Australian Industry Participation scheme, introduced by the Howard government in 2001, currently applies to Commonwealth procurements worth $20 million or more, and criticised the government for cutting $25 million from Export Market Development Grants while accumulating $192 billion in debt and offsetting $98.2 million in new spending with an uncosted $1 billion research and development cut.

Summed up the debate on the Australian Jobs Bill, confirming any domestic project worth $500 million or more must produce an Australian Industry Participation Plan, and said Senate committee consultations showed strong stakeholder support for the new Australian Industry Participation Authority established to administer the scheme.

Agreed with the previous speaker's criticism but attributed the destruction of manufacturing instead to the Treasurer letting the dollar rise from 52c to 90c, which he said halved the income of every manufacturer.

The Australian Jobs Bill 2013 was opposed as unlikely to create jobs, with the government's carbon tax, mining tax, and increased costs blamed for job losses in the steel, car, and food-processing industries.

The Australian Jobs Bill 2013 was debated, with opposition senators arguing it imposes additional costs and bureaucracy on business and cuts $1.1 billion from R&D, while crossbench senators Xenophon and Madigan supported lowering the major project threshold from $500 million to $20 million and adding anti-dumping requirements; the bill passed a second reading after the Greens withdrew their amendments.
